newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore "arrogance" haunts ties with neighbours.
newsitem.headline: Singapore "arrogance" haunts ties with neighbours.

text.p: Recurring spats with other countries are giving Singapore a bad reputation as a nation whose riches have made it arrogant and prone to treat its neighbours as inferior, regional analysts said.

Disputes over the years with the Philippines and Thailand were followed recently by Malaysian fury over a remark by Singapore elder statesman Lee Kuan Yew that Malaysia's Johor state was "notorious for shootings, muggings and car-jackings".
In language unheard in the 30-year history of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), Malaysian demonstrators called Lee "senile" and a "stupid pig."
The row died down last week after Lee apologised, but Malaysia said it would take time for ties to improve.

"There is a general feeling that Singapore is a little bit too assertive and too proud of itself because it is the richest nation in ASEAN," Christianto Wibisono, director of the Indonesian Business Data Centre, told Reuters in an interview.

"There has to be some serious soul-searching in Singapore on the way it handles relations with close friends and neighbours," said Mohamed Jabbar Hassan of the Institute for Strategic and International Studies in Kuala Lumpur.
Analysts in Singapore refused to comment on the issue.
"I do not want to comment on that. You can ask me about any other issue, but not that issue. I'm sorry," one analyst said.
The Singapore government also declined comment.
But Singapore's Straits Times newspaper said in an editorial on Saturday that Malaysia should rein in those calling for retaliation such as a cut-off of the water supplies on which Singapore depends.
"These smack of bullying and no self-respecting Singaporean will put up with it," the newspaper said.
"Mr Lee did cause offence," it said. "But the excessive Malaysian reaction has been no less hurtful to Singaporean feelings."

Singapore had a damaging row in March 1995 with the Philippines -- an ASEAN member along with Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam -- over the hanging of Filipina maid Flor Contemplacion, a convicted murderer.
The two nations recalled their respective ambassadors at the height of the row although relations were later patched up.
Ties with Thailand also hit a rough patch after Bangkok was angered by Singapore's comments about Thai corruption and the way Thailand is often depicted in the Singapore press.
Periodic disputes have also flared up over the treatment of the thousands of women from Indonesia and the Philippines working as maids in Singapore.
Some 28 Indonesian maids recently sought refuge in their embassy in Singapore, some complaining they had been raped, others that their salaries had not been paid.
Regional analysts said Singapore's propensity to hold itself up as superior grates on neighbours that are less affluent than the sophisticated city-state of three million people.

"I believe that if Singapore does not try to lessen its trouble-making with neighbours, it will be in trouble," said Chaiwat Kamchoo of the Department of International Relations in Chulalongkorn University in Bangkok.

Nelson Navarro, a columnist for the Manila Standard newspaper in the Philippines, said the row with Malaysia showed that Singapore's neighbors would only accept so much of what he termed bullying before they fought back.
Lee insisted his Johor jibe, made in an affidavit in a lawsuit, was never meant to be made public. The government insisted he was speaking as a private individual.
But Malaysia sees any comments by Lee, Singapore's founder and first prime minister and still a highly influential political figure, as reflecting the views of the government.
Wibisono said race plays a part in Singapore's arrogance.

"Singapore is considered Chinese by the other neighbours and I think this is the source of the problem," he said. "They feel a little bit superior, and the others are seen as inferior, because they (Singaporeans) are more industrious, productive and creative."
